title: How to Document a Store Tech Stack Before You Hand It to a Contractor
excerpt: Most store handoffs fail on undocumented decisions, not on code. This checklist covers apps, integrations, and recovery steps to write down before anyone else gets admin access.
body: Store handoffs fail on undocumented decisions, not on code. You hire a contractor to fix one thing, they change a template that three apps depend on, and nobody can say why it broke. The reason is rarely incompetence. It is that the real structure of the store lives in your head: which app owns inventory, which fields are safe to edit, which integration nobody has touched in a year. Writing it down takes an afternoon and turns the next handoff from a rescue into a normal job. This is the checklist worth doing before anyone else gets admin access.

Start with an app inventory. One row per app containing what it does in one sentence, who installed it, what it costs, when it renews, and who holds the credentials. The one sentence forces you to confront redundancy, and most stores find at least two apps doing overlapping work. Mark each app as load bearing or cosmetic. Load bearing means removing it breaks something a buyer would notice: checkout, shipping rates, email capture, subscriptions. That column is what you hand a contractor first, because it tells them what not to touch on day one.

Then draw the integration map. For each of five objects, meaning product, price, inventory, customer, and order, name the single system that is the source of truth. Most stores have two answers for at least one of them, and that ambiguity is exactly where sync bugs live. If a supplier feed writes price while your theme reads price from a metafield, write that down explicitly. Note where each integration is configured too, since a broken connection is usually an expired credential in a settings screen nobody remembers opening.

Document the theme and any custom code. Which sections are safe to edit, which are generated, which templates share a file, and how a change actually reaches production. If deploys happen through a theme editor, say so, because a contractor may otherwise build locally and overwrite live work. Keep a short list of known fragile spots: a hardcoded shipping message, a discount script, a section that breaks when a product has a single variant. These are the things that turn a small request into a rollback.

Write a runbook for failure. Where the order export lives, how often backups run, how to restore the last known good theme, and who to call for payment or fulfillment problems. Include the recovery step for the two failures that actually happen, a broken checkout and a broken product import. A runbook is not for the person who built the store, it is for the person on their third day who needs to stop the bleeding. Assume they will read one page, so put recovery steps above explanation.

Finish with access hygiene. Give the least privilege that gets the job done, use named staff accounts instead of shared logins, and remove access the day an engagement ends rather than when you remember. Keep credentials somewhere that survives a laptop change, and rotate anything that has been pasted into a chat thread. Documentation goes stale, so date every page and revisit it after any major change.
